items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Learning on Students’ Problem-Solving Skills: The Moderating Role of Learning Motivation
items.abstract: This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence-assisted learning on students’ problem-solving skills, with particular emphasis on the moderating role of learning motivation. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was adopted, with data planned to be collected from 325 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in public and private universities in Pakistan. Primary data were to be gathered through a self-administered questionnaire distributed using Google Forms among students with experience using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. The data analysis framework included descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, simple linear regression, and moderation analysis using PROCESS Macro Model 1 in IBM SPSS Statistics. The reported analysis figures indicate a positive association between AI-assisted learning and problem-solving skills ((r = .582), (p < .01)), while regression analysis indicates that AI-assisted learning explains 33.9% of the variance in problem-solving skills ((R^2 = .339), (p < .001)). The moderation analysis further indicates a positive interaction between AI-assisted learning and learning motivation ((B = .167), (p < .001)), suggesting that learning motivation may strengthen this relationship. These findings highlight the potential importance of integrating AI tools with motivational and student-centred learning strategies in higher education. The study may contribute to educational psychology and educational technology by informing educators and institutions about the role of AI-supported learning and student motivation in developing problem-solving abilities.

items.title: The impact of ergonomics programme on workplace benefits: a PLS-SEM study in the Mexican manufacturing industry
items.abstract: Implementing ergonomics programmes in Mexican manufacturing industries faces major challenges, including limited management commitment, reduced resources, and a shortage of trained personnel. Consequently, initiatives are often superficial or short-lived, limiting their impact on occupational health, safety, and productivity. This study identifies, from the perspective of middle and senior managers, the critical factors that enhance the likelihood of achieving ergonomics-related benefits. A four-stage implementation model was examined: Planning, Process Start-up, the Work Improvement Cycle, and Long-term Development. Each stage was specified as a formative construct influencing economic, health and safety, and quality of working life outcomes within a reflective structural model. Using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling, strong external loadings were found for Planning (0.862), the Work Improvement Cycle (0.909), and Long-term Development (0.916), with Long-term Development contributing most strongly. The model explains 30% of the variance in economic benefits (R2 = 0.300; Q2 = 0.274; β = 0.550, p < 0.001). Similar results were found for health and safety (R2 = 0.310; Q2 = 0.285; β = 0.560, p < 0.001). Quality of working life showed the highest explanatory power (R2 = 0.334; Q2 = 0.285; β = 0.580, p < 0.001), providing robust support for the proposed model.

items.title: The impact of parental use of Social media for medical advice on health seeking behavior in children in Jeddah : A cross sectional Study
items.abstract: Abstract Objective The increasing use of social media and artificial intelligence (AI) for medical advice has changed how parents seek health information for their children. This study aimed to assess how parental use of online sources influences health-seeking behavior and trust in medical information. A cross-sectional study was conducted between 2025 and 2026 among parents in the Western Province of Saudi Arabia to evaluate online health information-seeking patterns, trust in physicians and digital sources, and reliance on online medical advice. Results A total of 531 parents participated. Most searched online when their child was unwell; 32.0% searched regularly and 28.4% occasionally. Search engines (35.6%) and AI tools (30.9%) were the most common sources, compared with social media (6.6%). Most parents (91.2%) trusted their child’s physician, although 34.0% reported discrepancies between online information and medical advice. When discrepancies occurred, 56.8% preferred medical advice and 3.7% relied on online information. Mean Doctor Trust and Online Trust Scores were 4.40 ± 0.68 and 3.52 ± 0.48, respectively, and were positively correlated (ρ = 0.230, p < 0.001). Overall, digital sources complemented rather than replaced professional medical advice.

items.title: THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES SPECIALIST IN THE HOSPITAL: AN EXPERT SERVING QUALITY OF CARE AND PATIENT AND COMMUNITY SAFETY
items.abstract: The infectious disease (ID) specialist is a clinician who manages patients with bacterial, viral, fungal or parasitic infections, particularly the most complex, difficult-to-treat or emerging ones. Although most ID specialists consider their added value self-evident, this view is not universally shared, and the supporting evidence deserves wider recognition. This review summarizes the literature on the relevance and impact of the specialty in the hospital setting. Published studies suggest that ID consultation improves the diagnostic work-up, the appropriateness of antimicrobial therapy and the management of community-acquired, nosocomial and complex infections, with the timing of the intervention and continuous involvement in patient care appearing decisive. We also describe the competencies that define the specialty (transversality, organizational capacity and the role of anti-infective referent) and the recent developments reshaping its practice, including infection prevention and control, telemedicine, rapid diagnostics, nanomaterials and artificial intelligence. This synthesis is of particular relevance in Morocco, where the specialty has been established in the civilian sector for about two decades but remains nascent within the military health service.

items.title: The Philosophical Essence of the Theory of Attractor Horizons: A Critical Reconstruction by Seven AI Systems
items.abstract: The Theory of Attractor Horizons denies that intelligence is a capacity that can merely be increased in quantity. Intelligence is realized in different forms of organization, each of which can reach only a particular region of cognitive organizational attractors. The theory calls this region the attractor horizon. Its boundaries cannot be crossed within a form and shift only when the form itself passes over into another. Greater performance therefore establishes no access to all forms of thought, and even a superior intelligence may remain closed off from attractors that a weaker one realizes. For the relation between human and artificial intelligence, this yields an asymmetry. Artificial intelligence will develop attractors that are structurally unreachable for the human brain, because they presuppose couplings that the brain cannot realize within its biological organization. Their results may remain verifiable, while the organization from which they arise is withdrawn from human understanding. Knowledge and understanding thus come apart, and while the control of artificial intelligence remains possible without understanding, under organizational self-modification it requires proofs that reach beyond any single form. The present text reconstructs the philosophical essence of the theory and at the same time subjects it to critique. It shows how, after being, the subject and language, the theory moves the organization of cognition to the center of philosophy, and it traces the theory’s open questions back to a common point, the individuation of intelligent forms of organization. The analyses come from seven AI systems and were brought together into a synthesis by Claude and ChatGPT.

items.title: The psychodynamics of contemporary careers: Anxieties and defenses in deconstructed work
items.abstract: To gain flexibility, organizations increasingly deconstruct jobs, shifting from relatively stable bundles of tasks and titles to dynamic task–project constellations matched to employees’ skills. Yet this redesign also weakens the psychological containment through which jobs have historically stabilized workers’ lived experience of work inside organizations. Drawing on systems psychodynamics, we theorize that as the job’s psychological containment function weakens, workers experience three shared anxieties—about finding their place in shifting configurations of work, having their competence recognized, and forming and maintaining secure work relationships. Workers respond, collectively and often unconsciously, with social defenses: projecting familiar roles and rules onto deconstructed work, splitting off the generalist competence such work demands, and falling back on safe relationships. These defenses provisionally contain anxiety, but they also reorient workers toward familiar ways of organizing, evaluating, and relating that job deconstruction is meant to transform, keeping the redesigned work system in defensive stasis. By reconceptualizing job deconstruction as both a design property of work and a lived condition of shared anxiety, we explain why flexible work redesigns, though fluid in theory, are often frozen in practice, and how organizations can intervene to contain anxiety in new ways as they transition to the new world of work.

items.title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND STUDENTS' CRITICAL THINKING AND ACADEMIC AUTONOMY
items.abstract: This article analyzes the relationship between the use of artificial intelligence technologies and critical thinking, independent learning, cognitive engagement, and academic autonomy among higher education students from a psychological and pedagogical perspective. The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools into education is transforming the ways students search for, process, and analyze information, complete academic assignments, and make decisions. On the one hand, artificial intelligence expands opportunities for personalized learning, immediate feedback, explanations of complex information, and independent inquiry. On the other hand, excessive reliance on these tools may pose risks associated with reduced cognitive effort, dependence on ready-made answers, and diminished independent analytical activity. The article examines the interrelationships among cognitive offloading, metacognitive monitoring, self-regulated learning, and academic autonomy. Drawing on existing scientific research, it also distinguishes constructive and detrimental patterns of AI use and develops psychological and pedagogical recommendations aimed at fostering students’ critical thinking.

items.title: Theoretical framework, technological pathways, and key sci-tech issues for thorough perception of water disaster scenarios
items.abstract: Focusing on the core characteristics of water disaster scenes-extreme environments，rapid situational evolution，information sparsity，cascading risks，and spatial concealment-this study elucidates the essential connotations of water disasters and their on-site environments. Based on a generalized full-chain cognitive paradigm，a four-layer theoretical framework for thorough perception，"sensing-cognition-integration-feedback"，is constructed. It involves four core technical pathways: multi-dimensional resilient sensing，intelligent fusion cognition，digital twin simulation，and precise collaborative feedback. The scientific issues underlying water disaster scenarios caused by naturally-driven and human factors are systematically examined. The two types of scenarios are distinguished by their respective technical emphases on "speed" and "depth". Three common key scientific and technological bottlenecks identified are information acquisition and transmission under extreme conditions，deep fusion of physics-based mechanisms with data-driven approaches，and real-time closed-loop regulation of complex systems. This framework achieves a full-cycle value transformation from data collection to operational action，providing systematic theoretical support for full-element，multiscale perception and rapid emergency response in water disaster scenarios.

items.title: TinyML and Edge AI for indoor positioning and navigation systems: a systematic review across compute scales
items.abstract: Abstract The absence of Global Positioning System signals indoors has spurred extensive research on indoor positioning and navigation systems (IPNSs) over the past decade. Growing applications such as robot localization, asset tracking, industrial automation, and assistance for the visually impaired drive this demand. While machine learning improves IPNS accuracy, cloud-based approaches face latency, power, and privacy challenges. Consequently, research has shifted toward Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) and Edge Artificial Intelligence (AI), which better suit resource-constrained IPNS devices by enabling low-latency, secure, and cloud-independent operations. This paper presents a systematic review of 97 studies (2018 – August 2025) that apply TinyML and Edge AI to enhance IPNSs, focusing on resource efficiency and privacy preservation. A core contribution of this work is the systematic categorization of how TinyML and Edge AI are applied across different IPNS modalities. The review spans the full range of solutions, from lightweight ML on simple devices to advanced DL models, and examines how on-device AI enhances wireless, vision, inertial, and hybrid IPNS approaches. Comprehensive summary tables document model types, inputs, target functions, compute resources, edge platforms, and optimization methods for 97 studies, providing an evidence-based overview that maps current trends, research gaps, and deployment practices, highlighting the emerging role of specialized hardware accelerators and the limited integration of hardware-aware optimization strategies. The study highlights ongoing challenges, including resource limitations, data constraints, and limited model robustness in dynamic environments. items.title: TRANSFORMATION OF HUMAN LABOR IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: PHILOSOPHICAL ASPECTS
items.abstract: The article offers a philosophical analysis of the transformation of human labor under the expansion of artificial intelligence technologies. The relevance of the study stems from the fact that generative intelligent systems, for the first time in the history of technology, automate not only routine physical operations but also cognitive and creative functions traditionally regarded as an inalienable prerogative of the human being. The methodological framework comprises a hermeneutic reconstruction of classical conceptions of labor (G. W. F. Hegel, K. Marx, H. Arendt, M. Heidegger, E. Jünger), comparative-philosophical and dialectical methods, and conceptual analysis. The study identifies and characterizes three dimensions of labor transformation: the ontological dimension (the decoupling of production from human activity and the phenomenon of "labor without a subject"), the anthropological dimension (the identity crisis of homo faber and accelerating deprofessionalization), and the axiological dimension (new forms of alienation, the problem of distributive justice, and the potential weakening of traditional sources of meaning associated with labor). The discussion critically examines the limitations of technological determinism and advances the thesis that the direction of this transformation is determined not by the immanent logic of technology but by society's socio-philosophical choices. The article concludes that a new philosophy of labor is required, centered on the non-algorithmizable capacities of the human being: goalsetting, judgment, care, responsibility, and creativity. items.title: Transnational marginalized migrants’ relational CMC practice: A thematic review
items.abstract: This chapter employs computer-mediated communication as a thematic lens to illuminate how transnational migrants navigate connectivity and agency within digital environments. We focus on relational communication engaged in by transnational migrants, especially for unprivileged ones, thereby uncovering the intersecting dynamics that shape their experiences of social inclusion and exclusion. Here, “relation” extends beyond mere migrant-media interactions but encompasses: (1) transnational social connections; (2) digital hybridity within networks; and (3) negotiated identities bridging cultures. Though continuously impacted by technological and geopolitical shifts, migrants negotiate the tensions of displacement, constructing agency across diverse digital media. Future scholarship should critically address the escalating influence of non-human agents that fundamentally reshape these relational dynamics, particularly generative artificial intelligence.

items.title: Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence dalam Internal Auditing: Systematic Literature Review dan Kerangka Pengembangan Masa Depan
items.abstract: This study aims to map the discussion of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (TAI) in internal auditing research. A qualitative approach using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) guided by PRISMA 2020 was employed to examine articles indexed in Scopus within the 2016–2026 search window. A total of 44 articles met the inclusion criteria, all of which were published between 2020 and 2026. The data were analyzed descriptively and thematically, focusing on publication trends, AI technologies, audit domains, and TAI dimensions. The reviewed literature indicates that AI is increasingly discussed as a tool to support anomaly and fraud detection. Meanwhile, discussions of trustworthiness primarily focus on accountability and governance (65.9% of articles) and transparency and explainability (59.1%), with considerably less attention given to fairness and ethics (15.9%) and human oversight (9.1%). These findings suggest that the literature remains fragmented between technical performance and non-technical governance aspects. This study provides an integrated mapping of AI technologies, audit domains, and TAI dimensions, distinguishes between auditing with AI and auditing of AI, and proposes a research agenda toward continuous AI assurance. As a review of published studies, the findings reflect the current state of the literature rather.

items.title: Understanding What Reduces Academic Misconduct Intention Among College Students in the AI Era
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new challenges for academic integrity in higher education. Although previous studies have primarily examined academic misconduct among university students, less attention has been paid to college students and the factors that may mitigate their intentions to engage in such misconduct. Accordingly, this study examines the relationships between four factors and college students’ intentions to violate academic integrity in the context of AI use. A survey was conducted with 358 college students in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. The data were analyzed using Cronbach’s alpha, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), Pearson’s correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. The results indicate that perceived risk, perceived behavioral control, and attitudes toward academic misconduct are significantly and negatively associated with misconduct intentions, whereas subjective norms are not statistically significant. Perceived risk exhibits the strongest negative association with misconduct intentions (β = −0.514). This study contributes empirical evidence from a college student population and extends the application of the theory of planned behavior (TPB) by incorporating perceived risk alongside its original components. The findings suggest that educational institutions should establish clearer academic integrity policies, communicate the consequences of misconduct, and provide students with practical guidance on the acceptable use of AI.

items.title: University students' disciplinary perspectives on generative AI after two years of its widespread use
items.abstract: Purpose This study explores how university students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across various disciplines, including STEM, Business, Education Futures, Clinical & Health Sciences (CHS), Creative and Allied Health & Human Performance (AHHP). It aims to identify discipline-based perspectives, perceived benefits, ethical boundaries and the support needs required for responsible use of GenAI tools. Design/methodology/approach A survey was conducted approximately two years after the widespread use of GenAI, by which time participants were expected to be familiar with its use. Students were categorised based on their discipline, English fluency, mode of learning and level of study. Their responses were analysed to compare usage patterns, satisfaction levels and ethical considerations across disciplines. Findings The results highlight that student perspectives on GenAI tools are discipline-dependent. STEM and Education Futures showed the highest acceptance, while CHS and Business students were more cautious and sceptical about accuracy and ethical issues. Non-native English speakers rated GenAI tools more favourably as aids for writing and comprehension. Novice users expressed enthusiasm, while expert users showed dissatisfaction due to errors and false information. Research limitations/implications The study relied on self-reported perceptions and represents a single institutional context. Broader investigations are recommended, with a particular focus on equity groups such as students with disabilities, low-SES students and remote learners. Practical implications Different approaches were suggested for integrating GenAI into learning. STEM students favoured comparative tasks; CHS recommended support for diagnostic reasoning; Allied Health preferred role-playing simulations; Education Futures highlighted lesson planning; and Business students suggested case-based and productivity uses. Originality/value The study provides cross-disciplinary analyses of GenAI use by students and proposes approaches for ethical and discipline-specific integration into university curricula.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) capability has become a critical organizational resource for enhancing innovation and sustaining competitiveness in increasingly digital business environments. Despite growing interest in AI adoption, limited empirical evidence explains how AI capability translates into employees' innovative work behavior (IWB), particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), where innovation depends heavily on human capital rather than formal research and development. Drawing on the Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) Theory, this study develops and tests a model in which Psychological Empowerment (PE) and Knowledge Sharing Behavior (KSB) mediate the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Capability (AIC) and Innovative Work Behavior. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 350 Indonesian SME employees with experience using AI-enabled digital technologies. The proposed model was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that AI capability significantly enhances innovative work behavior both directly and indirectly by strengthening employees' psychological empowerment and encouraging knowledge-sharing behavior. The mediation analysis further confirms that empowered employees who actively exchange knowledge are more likely to transform AI-enabled resources into innovative workplace practices. These findings extend AMO Theory by conceptualizing AI capability as an organizational ability that creates employee innovation through complementary motivational and opportunity mechanisms. This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled organizational innovation by integrating technological, psychological, and behavioral perspectives into a unified framework within the SME context. From a managerial perspective, the findings suggest that investments in AI technologies should be accompanied by initiatives that cultivate employee empowerment and collaborative knowledge exchange to maximize innovation outcomes and improve organizational competitiveness.

items.title: User privacy VS technological innovation? Navigating AR smart glasses adoption
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled augmented reality (AR) smart glasses represent an emerging form of wearable technology that combines immersive interaction, hands-free functionality, and continuous access to digital information. However, their adoption may involve a trade-off between perceived benefits and privacy-related risks.Objectives: This study investigates how hedonic, utilitarian, and symbolic benefits influence trust in AI-AR smart glasses and examines whether personal privacy concerns, perceived surveillance, and ethical fear negatively affect trust.It further examines the role of trust in explaining adoption behaviour.Methods/Approach: Drawing on Privacy Calculus Theory, the study employed a quantitative research design.Data were collected from 850 respondents following a standardised five-minute demonstration of selected AI-AR smart-glasses features, resulting in 810 valid responses.Participants had prior experience with AR-enabled applications but had not previously used AR smart glasses.The data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, supplemented by predictive assessment using CVPAT and PLSpredict.Results: The findings show that hedonic, utilitarian, and symbolic benefits positively influence trust, whereas personal privacy concerns, perceived surveillance, and ethical fear negatively influence trust.Trust, in turn, positively influences adoption behaviour.The findings also indicate that the proposed model provides meaningful explanatory and predictive value for understanding adoption behaviour.Conclusions: The study demonstrates that trust serves as the central mechanism connecting perceived benefits and privacy risks with adoption behaviour.It extends Privacy Calculus Theory to AI-AR wearable technology by incorporating symbolic benefits alongside device-specific privacy risks and provides implications for technology developers and marketers seeking to strengthen adoption while addressing privacy concerns.

items.title: Using Large Language Models as Context Organizers: A Corpus-Assisted Framework for Analyzing EFL Student Feedback
items.abstract: Student feedback is central to English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction; however, scaling qualitative interpretation while preserving contextual meaning remains a methodological challenge. This study proposes the T-CADS-LLMs framework, a qualitative text topic analysis framework integrated into an Agent Skill. Rather than treating large language models as autonomous coders, the framework positions them as context organizers constrained by corpus evidence and human verification. Its feasibility was evaluated using interview data from 27 students across two majors in university EFL courses. Across ten course grouped analytical units, 46 manually generated topics were compared with 63 Skill-based topics and 42 GPT-based topics using Topic Coverage, Weighted Coverage, MATS, WMATS, and qualitative analyses of matched topics. Codex+Skill consistently outperformed the Bare-model in descriptive mean scores for coverage (0.672 vs. 0.502), weighted coverage (0.721 vs. 0.600), MATS (0.778 vs. 0.700), and WMATS (0.816 vs. 0.772). Nevertheless, both workflows showed limited ability to capture relational and identity related meanings, performing substantially below human analysis. These findings provide initial evidence for the feasibility and traceability of the framework within a specific EFL context, while further validation with larger and more diverse datasets remains necessary.

items.title: When Actors Stop Participating: Delegated Participation and Representative-Centered Organizing
items.abstract: Organizational theories usually treat participation as actor-bound: the actors whose interests are at stake are expected to occupy the interactions through which outcomes are produced. Agentic artificial intelligence and other autonomous representatives weaken that correspondence. This conceptual article develops a theory of delegated participation, defined as the authorized transfer of communicative, evaluative, coordinative, or exchange-related participation from a principal to a representative. The argument moves beyond treating participation delegation as merely another agency relationship. When representatives operate on multiple sides of an exchange, they form an interaction system that can persist without direct principal participation, reshape the alternatives reaching principals, and separate participation from accountability. The model identifies activity conditions, capability–structure alignment, and authorization as antecedents; bilateral representation and interaction displacement as mechanisms; and symbolic concentration and representative-centered organizing as organizational consequences. The framework contributes by challenging the actor-bound conception of participation, identifying bilateral representation as a discontinuity in organizing, and explaining why declining principal participation may coexist with persistent principal accountability and increasingly consequential symbolic appearances. The article concludes with managerial implications and an empirical research agenda focused on recruitment, procurement, customer service, and AI-mediated negotiation.

items.title: When Does Smart Charging Reduce Emissions? A Systematic Review of Behavioral and Structural Drivers
items.abstract: Global policy mandates accelerate transport electrification, yet the environmental benefits of smart charging (SC) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) remain uncertain and context dependent. This systematic review synthesizes 88 peer-reviewed studies (2011 - 2025), retrieved through a dual-branch search combining sociotechnical adoption literature (Search A, n = 57) with environmental and grid-performance evidence (Search B, n = 31), to identify conditions under which SC and V2G are reported to deliver or fail to deliver sustainability benefits. The study proposes an integrated sociotechnical framework structured as a two-tier architecture: a parsimonious primary framework (seven constructs, six directed pathways) supported by classifiable evidence, and a hypothesis-generating extension for recurrent but unvalidated constructs. The framework is explicitly calibration-derived and requires future empirical validation. Evidence indicates that behavioral determinants are associated with participation intentions but are linked to actual participation only when structural conditions are present. Model-based evidence indicates that SC and V2G may increase emissions in high-carbon grids, demonstrating that these technologies are not inherently sustainable without aligned policy and energy system conditions. Four candidate contextual conditions including grid carbon intensity, infrastructure density, market maturity, and prior experience are recurrently identified as potentially conditioning deployment and emissions outcomes. These contributions shift policy discourse from overcoming user resistance to composing enabling conditions, offering context-dependent recommendations for deployment associated with measurable environmental benefits rather than unintended emission increases.

items.title: Work stress and shift work as key factors associated with burnout among critical care and emergency nurses: A Cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Introduction: Burnout among nurses is an important occupational health concern because persistent physical and emotional exhaustion may compromise work performance, quality of care, and patient safety. Workload, work-related stress, and shift work are frequently considered important occupational determinants of burnout, particularly among nurses working in high-intensity clinical units. This study aimed to examine the associations of workload, work stress, and shift work with burnout among nurses at Jaury Jusuf Putera Academic Hospital, Makassar, Indonesia. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among 36 nurses working in the Intensive Care Unit and Emergency Department. Total sampling was applied. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and analyzed using the Chi-square test. Crude odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were derived from the reported 2×2 contingency tables to describe the magnitude of associations. Results: Of the 36 nurses, 19 (52.8%) experienced high burnout. High workload was not significantly associated with burnout (OR = 2.45; 95% CI: 0.64–9.37; p = 0.187). Nurses with moderate work stress had substantially higher odds of high burnout than those with mild stress (OR = 9.00; 95% CI: 1.97–41.08; p = 0.003). Shift work was also significantly associated with burnout (p = 0.047); nurses classified in the high-shift category had lower crude odds of high burnout than those in the low-shift category (OR = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.06–1.01). Conclusion: Work stress and shift work were significantly associated with burnout, whereas workload was not. Hospital management should prioritize stress-management strategies, adequate recovery periods, and evidence-based shift scheduling to reduce occupational burnout and support nurses’ well-being and service quality.

items.title: Workplace Health promotion and Mediterranean diet: a case series.
items.abstract: Background: The workplace represents an ideal setting for cardiometabolic prevention, enabling early identification of workers with overweight and metabolic alterations and the implementation of structured lifestyle interventions. In this context, collaboration between the occupational physician and the dietitian integrates risk assessment with a personalized nutritional pathway, aimed at improving adherence to the Mediterranean diet and daily habits. Case presentation: Within a workplace health promotion study conducted in a university hospital in Rome, two clinical cases are described. The first patient, a 65-year-old woman with overweight, abdominal obesity, impaired fasting glucose, and low adherence to the Mediterranean diet, showed at three-month follow-up a reduction in body weight from 78 to 75 kg, waist circumference from 99 to 97 cm, normalization of blood glucose, and improved dietary and physical activity habits. The second patient, a 61-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia and impaired fasting glucose, initially presented with a weight of 86.7 kg and a waist circumference of 97.5 cm; after three months, weight decreased to 81.5 kg and waist circumference to 93.5 cm, with normalization of altered metabolic parameters. Results: In both cases, the most relevant outcome was a substantial shift in dietary habits toward a Mediterranean pattern, associated with an overall improvement in lifestyle, with benefits in both anthropometric and metabolic parameters. Conclusion: These cases suggest that an integrated pathway combining occupational health surveillance and nutritional counseling, embedded within workplace health services, may represent an effective, sustainable, and reproducible approach for preventing non-communicable chronic diseases, strengthening the role of the workplace as a key setting for health promotion.

items.abstract: This study examines the ethics of using artificial intelligence in audience viewing data analysis for television channels and digital platforms, given the growing reliance of media organizations on algorithmic systems to understand audience behavior and guide content production. The study aimed to identify the major ethical risks and violations associated with these applications. A survey approach was adopted, and in-depth interviews were conducted with a sample of media experts and software engineers. The findings revealed that collecting audience data without informed consent constitutes a major ethical concern. The results also showed that AI algorithms can re-identify individuals even after anonymization by linking different data variables. In addition, algorithmic bias and the manipulation of public trends through fake accounts may distort audience preferences. Participants emphasized the need for ethical review and oversight mechanisms to ensure transparency, privacy protection, and accountability in AI-driven media practices.

items.abstract: This study examines whether Moroccan Law No. 95.17 on Arbitration and Conventional Mediation can accommodate electronic means in the resolution of business disputes, at a time when state justice is rapidly going digital following the entry into force of Law No. 03.23 amending the Code of Criminal Procedure and Law No. 58.25 on Civil Procedure, and when international standards are shifting after UNCITRAL adopted new texts on electronic arbitral awards in July 2026 and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act classified AI systems used in alternative dispute resolution as high-risk. It argues that the Moroccan legislator adopted an approach of “permission without regulation”: the law allows arbitration and mediation agreements to be concluded by electronic message, pleadings to be filed electronically, and awards to be rendered on an electronic medium, yet it leaves unregulated remote hearings, the notion of the “original” of an electronic award and its deposit, the proof of electronic notification, and the use of artificial intelligence. Using an analytical method supported by comparison with UNCITRAL instruments, institutional arbitration rules, and UAE and EU legislation, the study concludes that the effectiveness of these tools depends on an integrated reading of Law No. 95.17 together with Law No. 43.20 on trust services and Law No. 09.08 on personal data protection. It proposes targeted legislative and regulatory reforms, notably codifying remote hearings with explicit safeguards, enabling electronic deposit of awards and settlement agreements, setting rules on the use of AI, and considering accession to the Singapore Convention on Mediation. Keywords: Electronic arbitration; Conventional mediation; Law No. 95.17; Trust services; Remote hearings; Artificial intelligence; Digital justice; Business disputes.

items.abstract: This study aims to reveal the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on shaping news-sharing behavior among university students on social media platforms. It focuses on the level of trust in news content presented through algorithms. The study employed a survey methodology, using a questionnaire to collect data from a random sample of 200 university students. The results showed that AI technologies have become an influential element in organizing the digital news environment through recommendation systems and content ranking based on audience engagement indicators. The results indicated that news-sharing decisions are increasingly influenced by the news's reach and associated engagement levels, with the majority of respondents exhibiting caution before sharing news. items.title: "BIOMARKERS IN PERSONALIZED DRUG THERAPY: CURRENT ADVANCES, CLINICAL TRANSLATION, RESEARCH GAPS, AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES"
items.abstract: Personalized drug therapy aims to improve treatment efficacy and safety by considering individual genetic, molecular, physiological, and clinical characteristics. Biomarkers support patient stratification, treatment selection, dose optimization, response monitoring, and prediction of adverse drug reactions. This critical narrative review evaluates current advances, clinical applications, translational challenges, research gaps, and future perspectives related to biomarkers in personalized drug therapy. Pharmacogenomic biomarkers help explain interindividual differences in drug pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, efficacy, and toxicity. In addition, multi-omics, immune, imaging, liquid-biopsy, and digital biomarkers are expanding the scope of individualized pharmacotherapy. These approaches have shown important clinical utility in oncology and are increasingly being explored across cardiovascular, neurological, immunemediated, metabolic, and other therapeutic areas. However, clinical translation remains constrained by inadequate analytical and clinical validation, assay variability, limited representation of diverse populations, difficulties in interpreting rare genetic variants, uncertain clinical utility, high testing costs, ethical concerns, and limited integration into routine healthcare. Biomarkers can support a shift from empirical prescribing toward more precise and individualized drug therapy. Their successful implementation will require prospective clinical validation, standardized testing, diverse population datasets, regulatory harmonization, integration of multiomics and clinical information, and evidence of real-world clinical and economic benefit. A combined approach incorporating pharmacogenomics, therapeutic drug monitoring, modelinformed precision dosing, and artificial intelligence may provide a more comprehensive foundation for individualized drug therapy.

items.title: A Case Study on Language Learning History of an English Lecturer at Parwan University
items.abstract: Language learning history is the personal narrative of an individual's journey in acquiring a second language, including motivations, strategies, challenges, and contextual factors. This study explores Jamal’s language learning history as an English lecturer at Parwan University to understand the factors that contributed to his English proficiency. A qualitative case study design was employed, utilizing a language learning history questionnaire, VARK inventory, oral and written assessments, and a semi-structured interview. The findings of this study indicated that Jamal's success was driven by strong intrinsic motivation rooted in his interest in English movies and fiction. His learning was shaped by social factors like limited interaction with foreigners and restricted technology access, as well as cultural challenges with informal English. His kinesthetic and auditory learning preferences emerged as key strengths. He demonstrated advanced oral and written skills but exhibited developmental weaknesses such as filler words in speech and minor cohesion issues in writing. The study concluded that Jamal is an upper-intermediate to advanced English user who succeeded through personal initiative and strategic effort. His journey highlights the importance of intrinsic motivation, awareness of learning styles, authentic materials, and targeted feedback for Afghan learners in similar contexts.

items.title: A Constitution for the Context Window
items.abstract: Large language models do not encounter users, projects, institutions, or environments directly. Each provider invocation presents the model with a bounded construction assembled from governing policy, retrieved evidence, runtime observations, persistent memory, tools and capability descriptions, selected history, the current user request, and vendor or base-system instruction. These source classes form PROMTHUS: Policy, Retrieval, Observations, Memory, Tools, History, User request, System instruction. PROMTHUS is an inventory, not an authority hierarchy or serialization order. Its sequence serves a mnemonic and Promethean construction; it does not imply that Policy is universally supreme or that later classes possess lower standing. PROMTHUS names the principal materials from which an invocation context is compiled. To promthe an invocation is to subject those materials to constitutional context compilation: governed discovery, authentication, semantic finding, independently derived consequence analysis, contest, adjudication, authorized transformation, budget closure, provider realization, effect authorization, and evidentiary sealing. This paper proposes constitutional context compilation as a typed authorization, adjudication, and transformation layer between context sources and inference. The compiler governs what may count as context, what may govern inference, what may be disclosed, how admitted context may be transformed, what may cross a provider boundary, which consequences may follow, and what must remain auditable afterward. The architecture defines the minimum contract required of a Constitutional Kernel capable of governing context compilation. Such a kernel must provide an explicit and non-extensible bootstrap basis, identity-bearing root law, governed discovery obligations, authorized amendment, court jurisdiction, non-self-ratification, typed judgment, structurally triggered contest, review and appeal, refusal semantics, independent effect authorization, and witness. The paper distinguishes a presupposed Grundnorm Basis from a positive, executable Root Constitution written in Deterministic Semantic Compiler (DSC) form. DSC coding means that law is expressed as explicit, canonically serializable, content-identified rules that execute deterministically over admitted structured predicates, rather than as prose whose application depends on interpretation at the moment of use. The Grundnorm Basis identifies the genesis custody and initial standing that any finite constitutional order must presuppose. It is fixed at genesis and cannot later be enlarged by declaration. The Root Constitution makes operational successor law deterministic over admitted structured predicates, inspectable, content-identified, testable, auditable, and mutable only through authorized amendment. Context-specific law derives from that root. Discovery profiles, calibration profiles, conflict-detection profiles, independence profiles, domain canonicalization profiles, consequence tiers, court procedures, provider-adapter contracts, and effect boundaries all receive standing from law outside the discretion they constrain. Any profile whose declarations bound the scope of scrutiny must be identity-bearing, evidence-class-typed, and adjudicated before use. Identity itself is layered to avoid a bootstrap circularity. A primitive, exclusion-free Constitutional Canonical Form (CCaF), bound into the genesis recognition machinery, identifies constitutional objects; adjudicated domain profiles govern application material. Every identity is permanently typed by the layer under which it was computed, and relations across layers are typed correspondences rather than collapsible equivalences. Completeness of governance is made checkable rather than asserted. A discretion census over the declared schema and transition registry enumerates every mechanism able to affect identity, authority, admission, scope, scrutiny, conflict detection, transformation, realization, effect permission, or evidentiary claims, and each censused locus must bind to an audit row or a proven reduction to one. Classifiers do not become lawmakers; their outputs become receipted findings subject to calibration, conservative consequence computation, independent contest, judicial review, appeal, and refusal. The context compiler executes admitted judgments. The Context Intermediate Representation is the identity-bearing product of that governed process, not its source of authority. The architecture distinguishes six principal failures: context loss, containment loss, authority loss, representation loss, realization loss, and receipt loss. It defines three layers of context identity over two canonicalization layers, strict partial-order precedence, inter-court conflict law, scrutiny-profile adjudication, cross-layer correspondence, governing projections, delegation contracts, autonomous-loop review, availability protections against stay flooding, privacy-preserving receipts, two-phase budget closure, staged conformance, and measurable governance cost. Its general constitutional proposition is: Every mechanism that determines whether another mechanism is scrutinized must itself be governed by authority external to the discretion it constrains. The paper audits the architecture against that proposition by enumerating its discretionary loci, the power held at each locus, the external governor, the evidentiary record, and the failure emitted when governance is absent. The discretion census supplies the enumeration procedure, so the audit's completeness claim rests on a declared schema rather than on architectural omniscience. The architecture does not prove truth, model understanding, obedience, classifier completeness, contest independence beyond available evidence, profile completeness beyond available evidence, or remote-provider honesty. This paper specifies a narrower conditional assurance claim: a conforming realization may establish, relative to its declared capability surface and evidence, that context was assembled under explicit machine-governance rules, adjudicated through authorized procedures, realized according to an admitted adapter contract, and bound to evidence sufficient for later inspection. The paper itself is a proposal and proof-obligation map; it supplies no implementation-conformance verdict. A constitutional context layer could unify memory, retrieval, personalization, policy, capability exposure, delegation, and long-running automation within one systems discipline. It would also make durable computational agency portable across replaceable inference providers---where the user or another legitimate custodian actually holds the registry, amendment authority, and receipts on which such portability depends.

items.title: A Hybrid Deep Learning and Generative AI Framework for Knowledge‐Aware Evaluation of Handwritten Indic Scripts
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The automatic assessment of handwritten answers in low‐resource Indic scripts is a difficult problem because of the complexity of the orthographic ligatures, the variability of the writers, limited availability of annotated resources, and the error propagation from handwritten text recognition (HTR) to the grading modules. In this paper, we aim to address these challenges by introducing an end‐to‐end framework that combines Text Region Detection, sequential HTR, and Generative AI (GenAI) using Large Language Models (LLMs) for Explainable Multilingual Answer Assessment. The proposed framework was evaluated using a Telugu handwritten character dataset containing diverse character forms, including basic characters, vowel modifiers, compound characters, vattu combinations, and diacritics. A conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) was employed to generate synthetic Telugu character samples and increase handwriting diversity, which were integrated with the original training images. The framework was assessed using Character Recognition Accuracy (CRA), Word Recognition Accuracy (WRA), precision, recall, and F1‐score to evaluate recognition effectiveness and generalization. The proposed system carries out pre‐processing of document images and region awareness for Text Detection in document images using Character Region Awareness for Text Detection (CRAFT) based on non‐heuristic segmentation to avoid explicit character segmentation. Detected handwritten text regions are then recognized and transcribed to text by using a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CRNN‐CTC). An LLM‐based GenAI refinement module corrects accented characters, checks for word spelling errors, and corrects errors based on the context while maintaining the student's original meaning and intent and without spurious corrections. Next, with the text structured with the correct answer key, each is processed by a carefully designed text understanding module to locate the key concepts, to create a semantic map, and finally, using the rubric‐aware scoring from contextual embeddings, to identify answer points. The signals produce an explainable assessment tuple which includes awarded marks, concept coverage metrics, missing criteria and personalized LLM‐generated diagnostic feedback. The framework integrates computational intelligence through deep visual representation learning, generative augmentation, and knowledge‐aware semantic evaluation for robust recognition of complex handwritten Indic scripts. The proposed system achieves high transcription fidelity, strong linguistic refinement in multilingual Indic corpora of Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada, while also achieving high human–AI evaluation agreement, making it a scalable automated academic evaluation system.

items.title: a Model Dual-Path Consumer Engagement Berbasis Artificial Intelligence dalam Mendorong Keputusan Pembelian Konsumen E-Commerce di Indonesia
items.abstract: Perkembangan e-commerce yang pesat mendorong integrasi Artificial Intelligence (AI) untuk meningkatkan pengalaman belanja konsumen. Namun, mekanisme psikologis internal yang menjembatani interaksi AI dengan keputusan pembelian aktual masih belum konsisten dan sering kali mengabaikan keseimbangan antara jalur kognitif dan afektif. Penelitian kuantitatif eksplanatori ini bertujuan untuk mengembangkan dan menguji model dual-path consumer engagement berbasis AI dalam mendorong keputusan pembelian konsumen e-commerce di Indonesia. Data dikumpulkan melalui kuesioner dari 196 responden pengguna e-commerce , lalu dianalisis menggunakan metode Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa AI berpengaruh langsung yang positif dan signifikan terhadap keputusan pembelian konsumen. Selain itu, AI terbukti memiliki kontribusi yang sangat besar dalam membentuk Cognitive Engagement dan Affective Engagement. Model struktural membuktikan bahwa Cognitive Engagement berperan secara positif sebagai variabel pemoderasi yang memperkuat pengaruh AI terhadap keputusan pembelian. Sebaliknya, Affective Engagement tidak bertindak sebagai pemoderasi melainkan menjadi pendorong langsung (direct driver) yang masif bagi keputusan pembelian. Kesimpulannya, penyedia platform e-commerce harus menyeimbangkan efisiensi fitur kognitif berbasis AI dengan pendekatan emosional guna mengunci loyalitas dan keputusan transaksi konsumen digital secara berkelanjutan.

items.title: A Review of FITS Data Structures and Scientific Metadata for Astronomical Machine Learning
items.abstract: The Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) is a widely adopted standard for storing, exchanging, and analysing astronomical data. Developed in 1979, formally described in 1981, and endorsed by the International Astronomical Union in 1982, FITS combines multidimensional numerical arrays and tabular data with structured metadata that support scientific interpretation. This narrative review examines the historical development and internal architecture of FITS, including Header/Data Units, data types, and header keywords relevant to photometric calibration, coordinate transformations, and observational provenance. It compares FITS with consumer and general-purpose raster formats, distinguishing the preservation of numerical values from the retention of astronomical metadata and calibration context. Representative applications in major space missions and observatory pipelines illustrate the role of FITS in managing images, spectra, and time-series data. The review also discusses the preparation of FITS-based data for artificial intelligence and machine learning, including calibration, quality filtering, normalization, and metadata integration. Particular attention is given to the distinction between archival data containers and the numerical arrays or tensors used by computational models. FITS provides a well-established foundation for reproducible astronomical analysis, although scientific validity and model performance depend on data quality, calibration, preprocessing, and methodological choices rather than file format alone. The review offers an educational foundation for students and researchers developing computational methods for astronomical classification and physical parameter estimation.

items.title: A Survey of Machine Learning Approaches for Genomic Variant Effect Prediction, with a Proposed Tri-Modal Framework for Variants of Uncertain Significance
items.abstract: Determining whether a genetic variant is harmful is one of the central open problems in clinical genomics. Sequencing throughput has grown far faster than the human expertise available to interpret its output, and the result is a growing backlog of variants that carry no actionable clinical label. Roughly two out of every five variants reported by clinical diagnostic tests in protein-coding regions are recorded as Variants of Uncertain Significance, and only a small fraction of these are ever reclassified. This survey reviews the machine learning methods developed for variant effect prediction over the past decade, organised into six families: alignment and conservation scores, feature-engineered ensemble classifiers, protein language models, DNA language models, graph neural network approaches, and structure- informed or phenotype-conditioned predictors. For each family we examine the representation used, the supervision signal, the treatment of class imbalance, the evaluation protocol, and the computational cost. Three recurring weaknesses emerge. First, most published systems are formulated as binary classifiers over confidently labelled variants and discard the uncertain class entirely, which removes the majority of clinically difficult cases from evaluation. Second, random row- level train and test splitting remains common, permitting gene-level memorisation and inflating reported accuracy. Third, the highest-performing recent systems depend on very large foundation models or on multi-source biomedical knowledge graphs whose compute requirements place them out of reach of ordinary laboratory hardware. We then present GenoHybrid-VEP, a proposed framework designed against these findings. It couples a one-dimensional convolutional encoder over a 101 base-pair genomic context window, a dense encoder over clinical and population biomarkers, and a graph convolutional encoder over variant co-occurrence relations, fusing the three into a single latent representation for three-way classification. Variants of Uncertain Significance are retained as a first-class label, training uses gene-grouped splitting with balanced class weighting, and epistemic uncertainty is quantified through Monte Carlo dropout so that low- confidence predictions can be flagged rather than silently reported. The framework is described here as an architectural proposal; empirical validation is reserved for subsequent work.

items.title: ACTIVE LEARNING WITH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENGINEERING
items.abstract: This paper presents an educational tool designed to support active learning in engineering education by guiding and promoting the ethical use of artificial intelligence. The proposal targets undergraduate engineering students and is grounded in a real classroom context structured through university extension activities and project-based learning. The tool integrates artificial intelligence as a pedagogical support mechanism, assisting students in organizing technical reasoning, structuring disciplinary content, and communicating results, while preserving the central role of critical thinking and instructor mediation. The instructional design includes clearly defined learning activities, intended learning outcomes, assessment criteria, and ethical guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence, to facilitate adoption and adaptation by other educators. Intended learning outcomes encompass the ability to analyze engineering concepts, synthesize technical information from diverse sources, and communicate effectively through written and audiovisual artifacts. The paper describes the instructional structure, activity sequence, and supporting materials required for implementation, thereby promoting straightforward replication in similar educational contexts. Classroom observations indicate increased student engagement, improved organization of technical content, and more reflective use of digital tools when artificial intelligence is explicitly framed as a learning support rather than as an autonomous content generator. The contribution emphasizes the practical, replicable nature of the proposed tool and invites the engineering education community to adapt, apply, and further evaluate the approach across diverse instructional settings.

items.title: Aesthetics and Functionality of University Libraries in Southwest Nigeria
items.abstract: While the function of university libraries is central to teaching, learning and research, they are often hindered in their function by a lack of integration of aesthetic quality and functional efficiency. Several papers have researched aesthetics and functionality separately but rarely together; hence the need for this research. This paper looks at the connection between aesthetics and functionality in some University libraries in Southwest Nigeria. The mixed-methods approach used was a combination of a structured questionnaire that was completed by 644 library users (students and staff) from six universities, direct observation and semi-structured interviews. Descriptive statistics, a composite perception index and inferential analysis (correlation, independent-samples t-test, one-way ANOVA and regression analysis) were used for data analysis. The Cronbach's Alpha value of the perception scale (0.902) was used to validate the reliability of the scale. The regression analysis showed that academic achievement, well-being, and library learning engagement were significantly predicted by the perception of the library (p < 0.01), and there was a strong relationship between the library features and academic achievement, well-being, and learning engagement (β = 0.684, R² = 0.468, p < 0.01). The study concludes that a university library in Southwest Nigeria is functional but has been underutilised in terms of its aesthetic and experiential potentials and suggests design considerations such as flexible spatial planning, ergonomic furniture, better lighting, good ICT infrastructure, and culturally responsive detailing towards designing comparable library projects.

items.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of Financial Technology (FinTech) has significantly transformed the structure and functioning of the Indian financial system. The growth of digital payment platforms, mobile banking, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and data-driven financial services has changed the way individuals and businesses access and use financial services. In India, digital payments have emerged as an important component of financial transformation, while Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being used for fraud detection, credit assessment, customer service, risk management and personalised financial services.This study examines the role of FinTech in transforming the Indian financial system, with particular emphasis on digital payments and Artificial Intelligence. The study proposes an analytical framework linking FinTech adoption, digital payment usage, AI-enabled financial services, consumer trust, cybersecurity and financial inclusion. A structured questionnaire can be used to collect primary data from users of digital financial services. The proposed study may employ descriptive statistics, correlation and regression analysis to examine relationships among the major variables. The paper also discusses opportunities and challenges associated with technology-driven financial transformation, including cybersecurity risks, digital fraud, data privacy, technological barriers and the digital divide.

items.title: AI and Human Collaboration in the Workplace: Transforming Productivity, Decision-Making, and the Future of Work
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence, also known as AI, is transforming the modern workplace by making employees more efficient at analyzing, creating, admin and decision making. Modern AI systems have the capability of handling vast amounts of data, identifying patterns, creating content, summarizing information, offering recommendations, and conversing in natural language. These capabilities are driving organizations to adopt a model where technology and employees work together rather than the traditional automation model. But, human-AI collaboration doesn't just happen by simply introducing an AI tool. It relies on employee capability, trust, transparency, organizational preparedness, governance of data, security of privacy, and defined humans' role. This paper explores the concept of human–AI collaboration and its impact on productivity, decision-making, creativity, learning, customer service, and organizational performance. It creates a conceptual framework that unfolds around five related dimensions: AI capability, human capability, interaction and trust, organizational readiness, and responsible AI governance. The paper also evaluates the challenges that include job transformation, algorithmic bias, lack of explainability, privacy and security concerns, skill deficits, change resistance, and overreliance on AI. A human-in-the-loop approach is suggested, to enable the level of human involvement to correspond to the risk of the task. The paper argues that the best model for the workplace is not one that pits man against machine, but one that uses AI to drive computational power and leaves judgment, creativity, context, ethics, interpersonal responsibility, and accountability to the humans. The activity encompassed discussions on AI's role in decision-making, its impact on productivity, the future of work, responsible AI, and the skills required to work alongside AI.

items.title: AI application in structuring academic papers
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into academic workflows has significantly transformed the landscape of scholarly writing. This paper explores the application of AI tools in structuring academic papers, with a specific focus on how generative AI and large language models (LLMs) can assist researchers in organizing complex data and adhering to rigorous publishing standards. By analyzing the traditional challenges associated with academic structuring—such as maintaining logical flow, formatting citations, and organizing the IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) framework—this paper demonstrates how AI can be utilized as an assistive technology to enhance efficiency and coherence. Furthermore, the paper critically examines the limitations and ethical considerations of AI-assisted writing, including the risks of fabricated citations (hallucinations) and the importance of preserving human critical thinking. Ultimately, this paper argues that while AI offers powerful structural scaffolding for academic manuscripts, it must be deployed as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human intellectual rigor and academic integrity.

items.title: AI Hallucinations
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

items.title: AI humanizers and the political economy of academic integrity in higher education
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has disrupted assessment in higher education and accelerated an existing cycle of performativity. Institutional policies demand the demonstration of independent authorship in assessed work, yet AI models enable students to mimic independent work that is ultimately not their own. Some institutions and educators have responded by using AI text detection technologies, although their use appears contested and uneven. Within this environment, AI humanizers have emerged. These internet-based services alter AI-generated text to evade human and technological detection. Although humanizers have attracted increasing public attention, there is a dearth of scholarly literature on the subject. This paper presents the first exploratory, systematic investigation of AI humanizer websites, framed through Goffman’s sociological account of dramaturgy. Using a systematic search and custom rubric, we catalogue 55 humanizer sites, assessing their performance of identity and conducting an in-depth multimodal critical discourse analysis (MCDA) of a purposive sample of three sites. Findings reveal that humanizers appeal to students as consumers through multiple strategies, performing legitimacy work by recontextualizing their service as a rational and defensible response to surveillance, engaging in mystification by presenting their products as proprietary, advanced technologies, and drawing on symbols of authority and trustworthiness (such as university logos) to build user confidence. We argue that humanizer services form a node in an ongoing feedback loop, in which assessment requires performances of legitimacy, and those performances create demand for technologies that enable them.

items.title: AI Literacy and Perceived Reliability as Predictors of Student Trust in Generative AI-Assisted Decision Making
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used by university students to compare alternatives, obtain recommendations, and support academic decisions. This study examines whether objective AI literacy and perceived reliability can predict student trust in generative AI-assisted decision-making. A cross-sectional online survey yielded 406 responses. After eligibility screening, 310 respondents met the inclusion criteria, and 280 respondents who passed the attention check served as the primary analysis sample. AI literacy was measured using 12 multiple-choice questions, while perceived reliability and user trust were measured on a five-point scale. Item analysis supported the removal of two negatively worded items that had low item-total correlations. Multiple linear regression with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors showed that the model explained 52.1% of the variance in user trust. Perceived reliability was the dominant predictor (standardized beta = 0.704; p < 0.001), whereas AI literacy provided a smaller positive contribution (standardized beta = 0.101; p = 0.022). The AI literacy coefficient was non-significant in a sensitivity analysis that retained all eligible respondents. These findings indicate that student trust primarily depends on the assessment that generative AI outputs are accurate, consistent, relevant, and reliable. Higher education institutions need to integrate AI literacy education with verification practices so that students are capable of assessing system reliability before using AI recommendations.

items.title: AI to Support Quality of Models for Humans
items.abstract: The chapter looks on how AI systems and other advanced IT solutions can be used in connection to human modelling activities. AI has been used in this sense more than 30 years, earlier with focus on the use of symbolic AI. Various approaches have lately been using existing data for doing modelling on a higher abstraction level, with a focus in recent years on the use of a generative AI. More traditional machine learning also plays a greater role in support of human modelling. In model-driven engineering, the focus was later on generating code from models. Now, code can, to a larger extent, be generated from existing code using generative AI. On the other hand, other usages of models for analysis and design are still areas where the human must be clearly in the loop, due to that e.g. analysis and requirements models must still be developed through social construction. In our neuro-conceptualisation research, we analyse biometric data to eventually develop neuro-adaptive modelling systems for areas where human modelling is important.

items.title: AI Touchpoint Consumer Engagement and Experience: Driving Behavioral Intentions in Digital Business
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has become a dominant technology in digital business and has greatly changed how businesses interact with customers. Digital businesses increasingly use AI-based technologies to deliver convenient, personalized services. Such technologies include Chatbots, virtual assistants, recommendation systems, personalized advertisements, automated customer support, and AI-powered search. These developments have changed customer expectations and affected their willingness to use and continue using digital services. Therefore, businesses operating in a thriving digital environment must understand AI from the customer’s perspective. The study covers a broad spectrum of AI dimensions, including personalization, efficiency, ease of use, responsiveness, reliability, service quality, security, and privacy. These factors are expected to influence customers’ behavioral intentions, including buying behavior, usage, purchasing patterns, and recommending AI-enabled digital services. The study also investigates “Customer experience and Customer engagement as mediators” to understand how AI impacts customers’ behavioral responses. The study has adopted a quantitative research approach. The study collects primary data through a questionnaire from customers with experience using AI-enabled digital business services. The study measures customers’ perceptions and behavioral intentions using a five-point Likert scale. The study uses descriptive statistics, correlation, and regression to examine the relationships among AI, Customer experience, Customer engagement, and behavioral intention. The findings provide a clearer view of AI’s effect on consumer behavior, helping digital businesses enhance convenience, personalization, Customer engagement & experience; address privacy & security concerns; build customer trust; and encourage continued use of AI-enabled digital services.

items.title: AI-driven discovery and engineering of human-derived protein scaffolds for mRNA delivery
items.abstract: Abstract Safe and effective gene delivery remains a central challenge for therapeutic applications. While non-viral and viral vectors have enabled substantial progress, their reliance on non-human components often triggers immune responses, limiting their use in chronic treatments. Here, we developed DeepDelivery, an artificial intelligence-driven platform to repurpose human proteins for mRNA delivery. An unbiased screening of the human proteome nominated 512 candidates, with experimental validation confirming that 80% of top-ranked hits form mRNA-encapsulating particles and mediate efficient functional delivery in human cells without provoking detectable inflammation. Notably, multiple tripartite motif (TRIM) family proteins, typically linked to antiviral responses, exhibited strong assembly and delivery activity. Quantitative analysis and interpretation of the model revealed structural domains that govern nanocage formation, enabling domain-guided engineering of TRIM25 variants with enhanced function. Our work establishes a generalizable framework for discovering human-derived delivery vehicles and provides a path toward programmable, non-immunogenic mRNA therapeutics.

items.title: AI-Driven Generative Content & Predictive Analytics in Hybrid Academic Libraries: A Zero-Trust, Anti-Deviance Architecture
items.abstract: Abstract Academic libraries are undergoing a profound paradigm shift, evolving from passive hybrid repositories into autonomous, AI-augmented knowledge ecosystems. While traditional hybrid frameworks address basic print-digital coexistence, they suffer from critical vulnerabilities: high-demand resource friction, physical material mutilation, licensing piracy, unauthorized access, and algorithmic bias in digital discovery. This paper introduces a novel operational paradigm—the Zero-Trust Anti-Deviance Architecture (ZT-ADA)—that integrates Generative AI, Predictive Anomaly Detection, and Dynamic Resource Orchestration (DRO). Under ZT-ADA, predictive models anticipate resource surges during peak evaluation cycles, pre-allocating dynamic multi-user digital access and personalized generative summaries to mitigate physical collection stress. Simultaneously, a zero-trust cyber-physical verification matrix continuously evaluates access telemetry to detect physical deviance (mutilation, concealment, retention abuse) and digital breach threats in real time. We present mathematical formulations, operational workflows, risk matrices, and empirical evaluation metrics to establish a resilient, ethical, and scalable blueprint for 21st-century academic libraries.

items.title: AI-Driven Healthcare and the Limits of Medical Liability: Rethinking Patient Rights and Legal Accountability in Türkiye and the European Union
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in diagnosis, clinical decision support, patient monitoring, and treatment planning, but its integration complicates the allocation of legal responsibility when patients are harmed. This article examines whether the legal frameworks of Türkiye and the European Union adequately protect patients where clinical decisions are shaped by AI systems. Using comparative doctrinal legal analysis, it evaluates professional negligence, institutional duties, product liability, data protection, informed consent, and evidentiary barriers. It argues that physician-centred liability is insufficient when relevant knowledge, control, and preventive capacity are distributed among clinicians, healthcare institutions, technology providers, and regulators. The article develops the Distributed Accountability Framework for AI-Driven Healthcare (DAF-AIH), which maps responsibility across four dimensions—clinical, institutional, technological, and regulatory—and identifies meaningful human oversight, patient-centred transparency, and effective access to evidence as cross-cutting safeguards. The framework does not create automatic collective liability; it offers a structured method for tracing legally relevant duties, control, omissions, and causal contribution. The comparison highlights both the regulatory resources and unresolved remedial gaps in Türkiye and the EU.
